plain_title: Dementia with vivid hallucinations and changing alertness
one_liner: A dementia with fluctuating attention, detailed visual hallucinations, and Parkinson-like movement problems.
in_simple_words: Dementia with Lewy bodies is caused by protein deposits (Lewy bodies) in brain cells. Its signature features are attention and alertness that swing from hour to hour or day to day, vivid and detailed visual hallucinations (often people or animals), Parkinson's-like stiffness and slowness, and acting out dreams in sleep. Memory may be less affected early on. It's the third most common dementia and often misdiagnosed. Some antipsychotic medicines can be dangerous in this condition, so an accurate diagnosis matters.
what_it_can_feel_like: Dad sees children in the garden who aren't there. He's not frightened by them. We've learned not to argue.
One day she's sharp, the next she can't follow a sentence. The swings were the clue.
The wrong medication nearly killed him. Finding a specialist who knew Lewy body was everything.
common_signs: Attention and alertness that fluctuate markedly, like switching on and off
Detailed, well-formed visual hallucinations, often of people or animals
Stiffness, slowness, shuffling walk, or tremor, like Parkinson's
Acting out dreams, sometimes years before other symptoms
Severe sensitivity to some antipsychotic medicines

myths_vs_facts.myth: Hallucinations in an older person mean psychosis or Alzheimer's.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Vivid visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness are a hallmark of Lewy body dementia, which needs different care.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Any dementia can be treated the same way.
myths_vs_facts.fact: People with Lewy body dementia can react severely to certain antipsychotics. Getting the diagnosis right is a safety issue.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's the same as Parkinson's disease dementia.
myths_vs_facts.fact: They're closely related and share Lewy bodies. The main difference is timing: in DLB, thinking changes come first or within a year of movement symptoms.

how_common.plain: Lewy body dementia accounts for roughly 1 in 20 to 1 in 10 dementia cases, and is often under-diagnosed.
how_common.figure: Estimated 5%–10% of dementia cases; higher in autopsy studies (DSM-5-TR text and reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, often help thinking and hallucinations in Lewy body dementia, sometimes more than in Alzheimer's. Movement symptoms may be treated cautiously with Parkinson's medicines. Antipsychotics are avoided where possible and used only with great care. Non-drug approaches for hallucinations, good lighting, treating sleep problems, and physiotherapy for falls all help. Specialist assessment is strongly advised.
evidence_based_options: Cholinesterase inhibitors, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Cautious treatment of movement symptoms; avoiding most antipsychotics
Treatment of REM sleep behaviour disorder and blood-pressure problems
Physiotherapy, falls prevention, and carer education
self_help_that_supports_care: Not arguing with hallucinations; reassurance and calm
Good lighting and reducing shadows at home
Lewy body-specific carer groups, which understand the swings

when_to_reach_out: If someone has vivid hallucinations, big day-to-day swings in alertness, Parkinson-like movement changes, or acts out dreams, ask for a specialist memory or neurology assessment and mention Lewy body dementia by name.
is_not: Hallucinations from delirium, medication, or eye disease aren't Lewy body dementia. Parkinson's disease dementia has the same pathology but movement symptoms come first by a year or more.
hope_note: With the right diagnosis and the right medicines, many people with Lewy body dementia see hallucinations ease and thinking steady. Specialist carer groups make the unpredictability bearable.
